summary: Atazanavir is an azapeptide HIV-1 protease inhibitor, usually boosted with ritonavir (or cobicistat) and taken with food once daily. It commonly causes benign indirect hyperbilirubinemia (jaundice/scleral icterus) and prolongs the PR interval (first-degree AV block). Acid-suppressing drugs markedly reduce its absorption and require careful spacing/dose limits.
indications: Treatment of HIV-1 infection in adults and pediatric patients (weight-based) in combination with other antiretrovirals
Antiretroviral-naive and treatment-experienced adults (boosted regimen preferred)

moa: Selectively inhibits the HIV-1 protease enzyme, preventing cleavage of Gag and Gag-Pol polyprotein precursors. This yields immature, non-infectious viral particles and suppresses HIV-1 replication. Co-administered ritonavir or cobicistat inhibits CYP3A4 to boost atazanavir plasma concentrations.

absolute: Co-administration with drugs highly dependent on CYP3A clearance with narrow margins (e.g., lovastatin, simvastatin, midazolam oral, triazolam, ergot alkaloids, sildenafil for PAH, lurasidone, pimozide, rifampin, St John's wort, alfuzosin, irinotecan with boosting)

preg: Boosted atazanavir is used in pregnancy when the benefit justifies the risk; do not use unboosted. Avoid co-administration with tenofovir DF or an H2-blocker in pregnancy unless dosing is adjusted per label; monitor maternal bilirubin and neonatal hyperbilirubinemia.
lact: Breastfeeding is not recommended for women living with HIV in settings where safe alternatives exist, because of the risk of HIV transmission and infant drug exposure.
renal: No dose adjustment for renal impairment. In treatment-naive patients on hemodialysis, avoid the combination with tenofovir DF; atazanavir is not significantly removed by dialysis.
hepatic: Use with caution in mild-moderate hepatic impairment; not recommended (or contraindicated for boosted use) in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C). Monitor liver enzymes, especially in hepatitis B/C co-infection.

major: Proton pump inhibitors - markedly reduce atazanavir absorption and may cause virologic failure; restrict and space dosing
Strong CYP3A inducers (rifampin, St John's wort, carbamazepine) - reduce atazanavir levels
CYP3A substrates with narrow index (simvastatin, lovastatin, oral midazolam, ergots, pimozide) - serious toxicity
Other PR-prolonging drugs (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin) - additive heart block
moderate: H2-receptor antagonists - reduce atazanavir exposure; require spacing/dose changes
Tenofovir DF - lowers atazanavir levels (requires boosting)
Tadalafil/sildenafil for ED - increased PDE5 inhibitor levels (reduce dose)
Antidiabetic and statin agents - dose adjustment
minor: Antacids - transient reduced absorption if not spaced
interactions.food: Take with food; food increases bioavailability and reduces variability. Avoid acidic/buffered antacid timing conflicts.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol; may add to hepatic stress.
interactions.diagnostics: Commonly raises indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin; prolongs PR interval on ECG.

monitoring: Total and direct bilirubin and liver enzymes at baseline and periodically
ECG/PR interval in patients with conduction risk or on PR-prolonging drugs
HIV-1 RNA viral load and CD4 count to assess response
Fasting glucose/lipids; renal imaging if stone symptoms
counsel: Always take with food and exactly as prescribed; missing doses can lead to resistance
Yellowing of the eyes or skin is common, usually harmless and reversible - but report it
Tell your provider before taking antacids or heartburn medicines (especially PPIs) - timing matters
Report rash, especially with fever or blisters, immediately
Report fainting, palpitations or severe abdominal/flank pain
pk: Plasma suppression of HIV replication within days; viral load falls over weeks
Approximately 2.5 hours after a dose with food
Store at 25 C (excursions 15-30 C); keep in original container
pearls: Indirect hyperbilirubinemia (UGT1A1 inhibition) is expected and benign - do not stop for isolated bilirubin rise
Prolongs the PR interval; use caution with other AV-nodal blocking drugs and in conduction disease
Boost with ritonavir (or cobicistat) for reliable levels; unboosted use is limited
Acid suppression (PPIs especially) is the classic cause of atazanavir failure - manage gastric pH carefully
Take with food; atazanavir absorption is pH- and food-dependent
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember with food, unless it is almost time for the next dose - then skip the missed dose. Do not double up. Maintaining adherence is critical to prevent resistance.
overdose: Experience is limited; expected effects are PR prolongation and asymptomatic indirect hyperbilirubinemia/jaundice. Manage supportively with ECG monitoring; atazanavir is highly protein-bound and not appreciably removed by dialysis.
